title: Expanded Form Splitter
context: Grade 5, the page on the expanded form of decimals. An adult sees three ways to write a sum. What the page is doing is showing what each digit is worth, in words, as a decimal and as a fraction, so that the number can be taken apart and put back. The place value form names places, so it is written with is.

writeup.why: Write a decimal in place value, decimal and fractional expanded forms, and write an expanded form back in standard form, putting zeros in missing places.
writeup.look: Digit tiles over a place strip at the top, three labelled rows of parts under them, and a tray of parts on the last phase.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Expanded Form Splitter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x sixty-four, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many parts the decimal splits into, one for each digit that is not 0. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x sixty-four, y 202. The digit tiles run across the top of the working area at y 230, each 90 across, deep blue, with the large near-black point between Ones and Tenths and the place strip under them at y 330. The three rows run below at y 410, y 500 and y 590, each labelled at x 110 with its form: Place value form, Decimal form, Fractional form. Each part slides down from the digit it came from and lands in its row joined by plus signs; the Place value form row opens with the word is. A zero digit's part drops a little way and fades to half strength beside the words adds nothing. The Join button sits at the right end of each row, and the total it gives lands green under the row. On the last phase the tray runs along y 660, and a place left empty between parts lights grey and takes a 0 labelled Place holder. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a point key, a plus key and a fraction bar key, for setting a decimal or typing a part or a standard form into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. A decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it. The result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum, a difference or what is left, is green, with its shaded parts. Ten of one place traded for one of the next, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written after the point to line decimals up is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded part stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the decimal point is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label, Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left or Place holder, before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last decimal with its three expanded forms under it, each joined back up to the same number.

writeup.delight: On the second phase, when the child taps Join, the parts of the row slide back up into their tiles one after another with a soft click each, and the decimal lights green as the last one lands.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with the tiles in place. On the first three phases a decimal sits on the tiles over the place strip, and the row for that phase's form is empty below it. On the fourth the place strip is empty and the parts of an expanded form wait in the tray. One thing moves, once: the Split button, or the first part in the tray, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.

source_tool.description: A decimal sits on large digit tiles across the top of the working area, deep blue, over a place strip naming Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths and Thousandths. A Split button pulls the tiles apart into three rows below, each part sliding down from the digit it came from and each row labelled with its form: Place value form, with each digit and its place name joined by plus signs and the row opening with the word is; Decimal form, with what each digit is worth written as a decimal; and Fractional form, with the places after the point written over 10, 100 and 1000. A zero digit drops out of all three rows and fades to half strength, with the words adds nothing beside it. A Join button adds a row back up and the total lands green under it, matching the tiles. On the last phase the parts of an expanded form wait in a tray; dragged up, each snaps into its place on the strip, and any place between them that nobody filled lights grey and takes a 0 labelled Place holder before the standard form is read in green. A number pad sets any decimal with up to three places and up to four digits before the point. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many parts the decimal splits into.
source_tool.art_direction: Three slips, one number / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: strips cut into ten equal parts, hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, place value charts with a column for each place, column sums with their points in one line, and measuring jugs, ropes and scales marked in tenths.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared or combined with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip in tenths has ten parts of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
The decimal point is drawn large and always sits between the ones and the tenths. In a column, every point lies on one vertical line.
A place value chart names every column above its digit: Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance.

Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a strip cutting into tenths, ten tenths sliding together into one whole, a zero appearing after the point, or a carry moving to the next place.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a decimal plays in a piece of working: every decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it, and every result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum or a difference, is green, with its shaded parts; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Ten of one place traded for one of the next place, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written at the end, after the point, to make like decimals is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. An unshaded part of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the decimal point itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at which digit each part came from.
voice.onNext: A new decimal. Say what each digit is worth first.
voice.opening: One decimal, ready to be split three ways.
voice.onFinish: Three forms, one number, and it went back together.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Split any decimal, or build one back.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has written one decimal on three slips, by places, as decimals and as fractions. The tool is what splits the number into all three at once and shows a zero digit dropping out, and what fills a missing place with 0 on the way back.

answer_key.rule: A decimal expands three ways. Place value form names each digit's place, and is written with is: a number is so many ones + so many tenths + so many hundredths. Decimal form writes what each digit is worth as a decimal and adds them. Fractional form writes each place after the point as a fraction over 10, 100 or 1000. A zero digit adds nothing, so its place can be left out. Going back to standard form, a missing place gets a 0.
answer_key.wrong: The tiles split again into the row the child was writing, each part sliding down from its digit, and the child's own row is kept beside it, so the child sees which part came from which digit. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The 9 is in the ones place: 9 ones.
The 4 is straight after the point, in the tenths place: 4 tenths.
The 7 is in the hundredths place: 7 hundredths.
items.question: Write 9.47 in place value form.
items.checkpoint: Place value form names each digit's place.
items.misconception: Naming the 7 as 7 tenths, which gives it the name of the place straight after the point, where the 4 sits.

steps: The 5 is in the tens place, so it is worth 50.
The 2 is worth 2, the 3 is worth 3 tenths, 0.3, and the 8 is worth 8 hundredths, 0.08.
Adding the parts gives the number back.
items.question: Write 52.38 in decimal form.
items.checkpoint: Decimal form adds what each digit is worth.
items.misconception: Writing 5 + 2 + 3 + 8, which gives every digit its own face value and adds up to 18.

steps: The 8 is in the tenths place, so it is 8/10.
The 0 is in the hundredths place and adds nothing, so it can be left out.
The 3 is in the thousandths place, so it is 3/1000. So 5.803 = 5 + 8/10 + 3/1000.
items.question: Write 5.803 in fractional form.
items.checkpoint: A zero digit adds nothing, so its place can be left out.
items.misconception: Writing 3/100 for the last digit, which skips the empty hundredths place and gives 3 hundredths instead of 3 thousandths.

steps: There are 4 hundreds, no tens and 6 ones, so the whole number part is 406.
There is 1 tenth and no hundredths, so write 1 in the tenths place and 0 in the hundredths place.
There are 4 thousandths, so write 4 in the thousandths place.
items.question: Write 400 + 6 + 1/10 + 4/1000 in standard form.
items.checkpoint: Going back to standard form, a missing place gets a 0.
items.misconception: Writing 406.14, which leaves out the 0 in the hundredths place and moves the 4 thousandths up into the hundredths.

teaching_notes: Say each digit's place value aloud before any form is written; the three forms say the same thing three ways. Write the place value form with is, since it names places, and the decimal and fractional forms as sums. A zero digit adds nothing, so its place can be left out of an expanded form. Going back to standard form, a missing place gets a zero, or every digit after it slides into the wrong place. Check any expanded form by adding it back up.
generation_prompt: Build an expanded form tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A decimal sits on large deep blue digit tiles across the top of the working area, over a place strip naming Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths and Thousandths. A Split button pulls the tiles apart into three labelled rows at once, each part sliding down from its digit: Place value form, written with is; Decimal form; and Fractional form over 10, 100 and 1000. A zero digit drops out of every row and fades to half strength beside the words adds nothing. A Join button adds a row back up, the total in green. On the last phase the parts of an expanded form wait in a tray and snap into their places on the strip, and any empty place between them lights grey and takes a 0 labelled Place holder before the standard form is read in green. A number pad. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of parts. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Split the decimal into three forms. Add each form back up. To go back, put every part in its place and fill any gap with 0.
